new_statements.quote: Stress is here taken to fall predictably on the first syllable of a word. Ultimately this analysis could prove simplistic because it entails that verb roots, which are relatively unstressed and show no vowel length contrasts, are at least phonologically part of the same word as whatever happens to precede them. [p.196] ... It also contains Rib (or 'Areba'), but only as a dialect that now appears to be completely indistinguishable from Kurtjar. [p.181] ... In any case, Rib will henceforth not be distinguished from Kurtjar in the present study. [p.188]

Ultimately this analysis could prove simplistic because it entails that verb roots, which are relatively unstressed and show no vowel length contrasts, are at least phonologically part of the same word as whatever happens to precede them.' new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the first syllable of the word (Kurtjar; Rib/Areba subsumed as an indistinguishable dialect). Vowel length in Kurtjar is confined to initial syllables (p.195), so the initial syllable is also the only possible long one. The analysis presupposes that relatively unstressed verb roots are phonologically part of the preceding word.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the author flags that the initial-stress analysis 'could prove simplistic' because verb roots are 'relatively unstressed' and must be treated as part of the same phonological word as what precedes them.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain explicitly 'a word' (phonological word); the hedge concerns whether verb roots form a word with preceding material. Two-paragraph synchronic sketch inside a historical-phonology paper, data elicited from the last speakers ca. 1970s. The sentence is written for Kurtjar; Black states (pp.181, 188) that the Rib/Areba data he, Sommer and Sutton recorded are indistinguishable from Kurtjar and that Rib is not distinguished from Kurtjar in the study, so no Areba-specific stress statement exists anywhere in the paper.
new_statements.identity_note: The only descriptive source (Black 1980) treats Rib/Areba (areb1238, AIATSIS Y107) as a dialect 'completely indistinguishable from Kurtjar' (Gurdjar, gurd1238, ISO gdj, AIATSIS G33) and explicitly does not distinguish it; the quoted stress statement is written for Kurtjar and covers the Rib data Black, Sommer and Sutton collected. The same statement therefore serves gurd1238 (currently the named source could not be reached in our source list) and areb1238 should be filed as a duplicate/dialect entry of gurd1238, not as an independent data point. Sister language Kuthant (kuth1240) is already in the catalog from the same PDF (weight-sensitive, p.197) and is a different rule.
